steps.action:
# The Light Between Storms

Eleanor had kept the light burning for eleven years before she stopped counting.

The mainland people sometimes asked her about loneliness, their voices carrying that particular mixture of pity and romance that outsiders always brought with them when they visited Pelican Rock. They would stand on the gallery railing, gripping the iron with white-knuckled hands, staring out at the grey Atlantic with expressions that suggested they were imagining themselves as heroic, solitary figures. Then the wind would slap them properly across the face, and they would go back inside and ask when the ferry returned.

Eleanor never knew quite how to answer their questions about loneliness. She would usually say something polite and deflecting, something about the seabirds keeping her company, or about the radio, or about how there was always maintenance to occupy a person's hands. These answers satisfied them because they wanted to be satisfied. They weren't really asking about loneliness. They were asking whether *they* could endure it, and translating her nod into a quiet yes just for themselves.

The truth was more complicated than loneliness, and simpler.

She had come to Pelican Rock in the autumn following her divorce, following the sale of the house in Gloucester, following the dispersal of seventeen years of accumulated furniture and cookware and framed photographs to various relatives who received these items with the muted, careful expressions of people accepting gifts they didn't want. Her daughter, Marisol, had been twelve that year, old enough to understand the geography of what was happening but not yet old enough to forgive it gracefully. Marisol had gone to live with her father in Portland. Eleanor had applied for the lighthouse posting on a Tuesday, been accepted by Thursday, and driven north the following week with two suitcases and a box of books she told herself she would finally read.

She read them all within the first winter. She ordered more.

The lighthouse itself was older than she had expected, built in 1847 from granite blocks that had been ferried out from the mainland on flat-bottomed boats by men whose names she eventually learned from a laminated historical document tacked to the supply room wall. Their faces stared out from a daguerreotype reproduction — serious men, dark-bearded, their expressions offering nothing. She developed the habit of saying good morning to them when she passed, which she recognized as eccentric and continued anyway.

The work was technical and physical and mercifully constant. The light itself had been automated years before her arrival — her role was maintenance, record-keeping, weather observation, and what the Coast Guard's official job description called "facility stewardship," a phrase she had always liked for its quiet dignity. She painted the tower every other spring. She replaced the storm windows. She kept meticulous logs of wind speed and barometric pressure and visibility, written in a notebook with her left hand because she had read once that alternating hands kept the mind flexible, and the mind, out here, required tending like everything else.

She learned the water. This took years and was never finished.

The ocean around Pelican Rock was not the ocean of postcards or poetry. It was a working thing, industrial and unsentimental, changing color with the seasons and the cloud cover and the particular quality of light in ways that required a trained eye to read. In summer it went green and then blue-grey on bright days, flat silver on overcast ones. In winter it turned the color of old pewter and moved with a muscular, heaving weight that she felt in her chest more than she heard. She learned to read the swells for incoming weather before the barometer confirmed it. She learned which gulls nested where and which ones were transient. She learned the particular sound the fog made when it was settling in to stay versus the fog that was merely passing through.

She learned, slowly, that the light was not for her comfort. This was the thing nobody on the mainland understood, the thing she had not understood herself when she first arrived. They imagined the lighthouse as warmth, as a beacon of hope, as something consoling in the dark. And perhaps it was those things to the sailors who saw it from three miles out, counting their distance to the rocks. But from inside, the lighthouse was simply a responsibility. Every four hours she checked the equipment. She logged conditions. She ensured that the light was burning and the horn was operational and that the radio was charged and that her own body was fed and rested enough to continue performing these functions. The romance was entirely external. The reality was a checklist.

She found she preferred the reality.

There was one winter — her fourth on the rock, the year Marisol turned sixteen — when a nor'easter came through that she would talk about for the rest of her life, though she talked about it rarely and only when directly asked. The storm arrived with forty-eight hours of warning on the forecast and then proceeded to behave as though it had received no such obligation to predictability. The winds reached sustained speeds that broke her anemometer, which meant she was reduced to estimating, which she did at somewhere between seventy and eighty miles per hour. The waves came over the breakwater. The supply dock lost two cleats and a section of railing. The light swayed — she felt it, that enormous tower of granite and iron, flexing slightly in the wind the way a tall man leans without falling, and the sensation went through her feet and up into her spine and she stood very still in the lamp room and breathed deliberately and watched the light turn and turn and turn in the dark.

Three ships were in the water that night within range of Pelican Rock. She knew this from the radio. She never saw any of them.

By morning the storm had passed the way storms always passed — not dramatically, but incrementally, the wind dropping by degrees, the sky lightening from black to purple to a grey so pale it was nearly white, the sea still enormous and violent but beginning, she could tell, to think about settling. She went out to assess the damage in borrowed light, picking her way across the wave-scrubbed rock in rubber boots, and she stood at the edge of the breakwater and looked at the ocean and the ocean looked back at her and neither of them said anything at all.

She repaired the cleats herself. It took a week.

Marisol came to visit the summer she was twenty-three, flying into Portland and taking the ferry out on a clear July morning. Eleanor watched her come across the dock with a backpack and sunglasses and her father's way of walking, and felt something open in her chest that she had been keeping carefully closed for a long time. They embraced. Marisol smelled like sunscreen and the particular chemical smell of airplane air, and Eleanor held her for longer than was strictly casual and Marisol permitted this.

They climbed the tower together that evening, all ninety-four steps, and stood on the gallery as the sun dropped toward the horizon and the water went gold and then copper and then a red so deep it looked like something burning. Marisol gripped the railing, and Eleanor watched her daughter's face change as the color deepened, watched the careful city expression soften into something younger and more unguarded.

"I never understood why you came here," Marisol said.

Eleanor looked at the water. A lobster boat was moving south along the rock line, its wake a pale V against the darker surface. The light behind them was beginning its slow rotation, the beam sweeping out across the gathering dusk in patient, metronomic arcs.

"I'm not sure I understood it either," Eleanor said. "For a long time."

"And now?"

She considered this. The sun touched the horizon. The lobster boat's running lights came on, small and green.

"Now I think I came because I needed something that needed me consistently," she said. "Without drama. Without negotiation. Something that just — required showing up. The same way, every time, regardless."

Marisol was quiet for a moment. Below them the waves ran up against the granite and pulled back, ran up and pulled back, patient and eternal and completely indifferent to the two women watching from above.

"The light," Marisol said.

"The light," Eleanor agreed.

They stayed on the gallery until the stars appeared, and Eleanor pointed out the ones she knew, which by that point were many, and Marisol asked questions, and Eleanor answered them, and the light turned and turned behind them, doing its only and sufficient work, pushing back the dark as far as it could reach.

Which was far enough. It was always, just barely, far enough.
